title: One bad tenant made me sell. Is 43 too late to build a portfolio?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #187 | MAKE PROPERTY INVESTMENT A DINNER TABLE CONVERSATION
excerpt: A 43-year-old sold his condo near an LRT station after a tenant broke the lease. Sean answers his rapid-fire questions on age, tenants, renovation budgets, price points and transit.

qa.asker: L, a viewer who wrote in on Facebook
qa.context: L is 43. He bought a condo next to an LRT station to rent out but struggled to find tenants at a good rent. An expat tenant asked for many new items before signing a one-year agreement, then left after two months without compensation, so L sold the property.
qa.question: Is 43 too late to build a portfolio, and how do investors handle rent collection, renovation budgets, bad tenants, price points and locations near rail?
qa.quote: Every location will have its median price.
qa.answer: It isn't too late, but it is harder: banks lend to about 65 or 70, so a shorter loan means higher instalments that rents struggle to cover. Sean builds equity slowly with units whose rent covers the instalment, uses a management company, and judges a price against the area's median rather than looking for the cheapest unit.

reasons.title: Deposits and stamped agreements protect you
reasons.body: The usual two months' deposit, half a month for utilities and one month in advance cover a tenant who breaks the lease early. A stamped tenancy agreement holds up better and lets you declare the rent as income for your next loan.

reasons.title: Furnishing budgets depend on use
reasons.body: For an investment unit, Sean puts a one-bedroom at about RM25,000 to RM28,000, and a larger unit with a better kitchen at about RM45,000 to RM55,000. A three-bedroom own-stay unit might be about RM80,000, and landed homes can cost far more.

reasons.title: Rent collection is active work
reasons.body: Well-presented units attract tenants who treat them well. Send a warning letter after the first missed payment rather than chasing six months later; passive income is not the same as doing nothing.

reasons.title: Transit helps only if it shortens the trip
reasons.body: A station is worth more when the CBD is a few stops away, parking is easy and malls and offices are part of the development. If the train takes an hour and a half, tenants will still drive.

actions: Collect the standard deposits and use a stamped tenancy agreement.
Act on the first late payment.
Find the median price per square foot for each area and aim below it.
Check how many stops and minutes a project is from the CBD, not just whether it has a station.
Work through Sean's four basic steps before choosing an area and project.
qa.caveat: Rail access isn't a guarantee: some new projects set the area's highest prices, while some pricier areas still rent best. Price point is always relative to the location.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #187. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in August 2022. Sean says he works at The Makeover Guys, a furnishing company; a property management company manages his units; and he learnt the median-price method from FAR Capital.
